label: thm-type-a
title: Theorem
body_md:
The type $\mathrm{A}_n$ Hall--Littlewood polynomial indexed by a rectangular partition of length $n$ satisfies the following dual Jacobi--Trudi formula:
\label{thm-type-a}
\[
P_{(k^n)}(X;t) = \sum_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{Z}^k\\|y|=0}} \det_{1\le i,j\le k}(t^{k\binom{y_i}{2}+iy_i} e_{n-i+j-ky_i}(X))\,.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Begin by expanding the Hall--Littlewood polynomial of type $\mathrm{A}_n$,
\[
P_{(k^n)}(X;t) = \frac{1}{[n]_t!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n} \sigma.\!\left( \prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\lambda_i}
 \prod_{i<j} \frac{x_i-t x_j}{x_i-x_j}
\right).
\]
When $\lambda = (k^n)$, then note that $\prod_{i=1}^nx_i^k$ is invariant under the action of the symmetric group. We get
\[
P_{(k^n)}(X;t) =\frac{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{k}}{[n]_t!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_n} \sigma.\!\left(
 \prod_{i<j} \frac{x_i-t x_j}{x_i-x_j}
\right)= \frac{\prod_{i=1}^nx_i^k}{[n]_t!} [n]_t!= \prod_{i=1}^n x_i^k = s_{(k^n)}(X)\,, 
\]
where we have used \cite[p. 207, (1.4)]{Macdonald1995}.

Now consider the right-hand side of the identity we aim to show, and factor out the power of $t$ to get
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:power of t A}
\sum_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{Z}^k\\|y|=0}} \det_{1\le i,j\le k}(t^{k\binom{y_i}{2}+iy_i} e_{n-i+j-ky_i}(X))
= 
\sum_{\substack{y\in\mathbb{Z}^k\\|y|=0}} 
\Big( \prod_{i=1}^k t^{k\binom{y_i}{2}+iy_i} \Big)
\det_{1\le i,j\le k}(e_{n-i+j-ky_i}(X))\,.
\end{equation}
If $y\neq 0$ and $|y|=0$ then there exists an $y_i<0$. We then have that
$$n-i+r-ky_i\geq n-i+r+k>n,$$
for every column index $1\leq r\le k$. Thus the $i$-th row of the matrix in the determinant is zero and subsequently the determinant vanishes and only $y=0$ survives.
An application of the 
dual Jacobi--Trudi identity \eqref{eq: dual JT type A} gives that the right-hand side is $s_{(n^k)'}(X)$, as claimed.

label: lem:powery
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:powery}
Let $A = (a_{ij}(x))_{1\le i,j\le k}$ be a matrix of univariate functions.
Let $R\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^k$ be a finite $S_k$-invariant subset of $\mathbb{Z}^k$.
Then,
   \[
    \sum_{y \in R} \det_{1 \le i,j \le k}
    (
    t^{jy_i} a_{i,j}(y_i)
    ) =  \sum_{y \in R} t^{\sum_{j=1}^k j y_j} \det_{1 \le i,j \le k} (
    a_{i,j}(y_j)).
    \]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand the left-hand side according to the Leibniz formula of the determinant,
    \[
     \sum_{y \in R} \sum_{\sigma \in S_k}  \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)  \left( \prod_{j=1}^k
    t^{jy_{\sigma(j)}} a_{\sigma(j),j}(y_{\sigma(j)})
    \right).
    \]
Let $\mathrm{sort}(R)=\{y\in R\mid y_1\geq \dots\geq y_k\}$ and define an action of $S_k$ on $R$ by $(\mu\cdot y)_i=y_{\mu(i)}$. Observe that any $y\in R$ can be written as $y=\mu\cdot x$ for some $x\in \mathrm{sort}(R) $ and some $\mu\in S_k$. Conversely from one $x\in \mathrm{sort}(R) $ we can obtain the same $y\in R$ multiple times by acting with different $\mu$'s. The number of times this can happen is given by the size of the stabilizer of $x$ under this action and denoted by $m(x)=\vert\mathbf{Stab}(x)\vert$. Using this observation, we can rewrite the above sum as
    \[
     \sum_{x \in \mathrm{sort}(R)}\frac{1}{m(x)}\sum_{\mu\in S_k} \sum_{\sigma \in S_k}  \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)  \left( \prod_{j=1}^k
    t^{jx_{\mu(\sigma(j))}} a_{\sigma(j),j}(x_{\mu(\sigma(j))})
    \right).
    \]
Summing over all $\rho=\mu\circ \sigma$ instead of $\mu\in S_k$, we obtain
    \[
     \sum_{x \in \mathrm{sort}(R)}\frac{1}{m(x)}\sum_{\rho\in S_k} \sum_{\sigma \in S_k}  \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)  \left( \prod_{j=1}^k
    t^{jx_{\rho(j)}} a_{\sigma(j),j}(x_{\rho(j)})
    \right).
    \]
The inner sum now clearly is a determinant and this is equal to
\begin{multline*}
     \sum_{x \in \mathrm{sort}(R)}\frac{1}{m(x)}\sum_{\rho\in S_k} \prod_{j=1}^k
    t^{jx_{\rho(j)}} \det_{1\leq i,j\leq k}\left( a_{i,j}(x_{\rho(j)})
    \right)
    =\sum_{y\in R}\prod_{j=1}^k
    t^{jy_j} \det_{1\leq i,j\leq k}\left( a_{i,j}(y_j)
    \right)\\=\sum_{y \in R} t^{\sum_{j=1}^k j y_j} \det_{1 \le i,j \le k} (
    a_{i,j}(y_j)),
\end{multline*}
    where the first equality again follows from the definition of the group action. This proves the lemma.

label: def: labelled graph
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def: labelled graph}
Set $\bar k=k+\lfloor h^++h^-\rfloor$ and $K=2(k+h^+)$.
The graph $\Lambda_{m,k,h^+,h^-}$ has vertex set
\[
 V=[0,\bar k+m]+|h^++h^-|
\]
and edge labels $E=[1,m]$. The edge labelled $j$ joins
\[
 k+j+h^++h^-\qquad\text{and}\qquad |k-j+h^+-h^-|.
\]
It is called a \emph{type-$1$ edge} if
$j<k+\lceil h^+-h^-\rceil$, and a \emph{type-$2$ edge} otherwise.
The vertices
\[
 c_j=j+|h^++h^-|,\qquad 0\leq j\leq\bar k,
\]
are the centers.

label: lem: Noodle-Doodle expansion first form
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Expansion over orientations

title: Proof
body_md:
Using multilinearity in columns $n-m+1,\ldots,n$, we expand the
left-hand side by choosing one endpoint of each edge. Orienting each edge
towards the chosen endpoint identifies the resulting terms with
orientations of the graph.

By the antisymmetry of the determinant, an orientation with a vertex of
indegree two gives a zero summand, since two columns are equal. In every
remaining orientation, a component with $r$ vertices has $r-1$ vertices
of indegree one and precisely one of indegree zero. Its edges are directed
away from the latter vertex. Hence it suffices to sum over
$\mathcal A(\Lambda_{m,k,h^+,h^-})$.

Changing the root from $c_j$ to $z_j$ reverses precisely the edges between
these two vertices. Thus the edges in $E_A$ contribute $p_s$, and all other
edges contribute $p_t$, proving~\eqref{eq: to show pure graph}.

label: lem: EA and tA(j) are given by
title: Lemma
head: environment
labels: lem: EA and tA(j) are given by

title: Proof
body_md:
We claim that \begin{equation*}
        E_A(c_i,z_i)=\left\{2(k+h^+)\ell+k+\alpha_i i+\lceil h^+-h^-\rceil-[y_i< 0]\lceil |h^++h^-|\rceil~:~
    \ell=0,\dots,|y_i|-1\right\},
    \end{equation*}
    from which \eqref{eq: EA is given by} immediately follows. 
    
    Note that if $z_i$ is located weakly to the right side of $c_i$ then the $|y_i|$ edges between $c_i$ and $z_i$ are labelled with $$2(k+h^+)\ell+k+i+\lceil h^+-h^-\rceil,$$ for $\ell=0, \dots, |y_i|-1$ as claimed. 
    
Similarly, if $z_i$ is located strictly to the left side of $c_i$ then the $|y_i|$ edges between $c_i$ and $z_i$ consist of the one type-$1$ edge labelled by $$k-i+\lfloor h^+-h^-\rfloor$$ and the $|y_i|-1$ type-$2$ edges labelled with $$2(k+h^+)\ell+k-i^*+\lceil h^+-h^-\rceil$$ for $\ell=1,\dots,|y_i|-1$. Here we denote by $i^*=i$ if $(h^+,h^-)=(0,0),\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2}\right)$ and $i^*=i+1$ if $(h^+,h^-)=\left(\frac{1}{2},0\right),\left(0,-\frac{1}{2}\right)$.
Note that $\lceil |h^++h^-|\rceil=1$ if and only if $(h^+,h^-)=(\frac{1}{2},0),(0,-\frac{1}{2})$ and this proves the first claim. Note that this also immediately proves the formula for $|E_A^2|$ as it shows that $E_A$ contains $|y_i|$ type-$2$ edges if $y_i\geq 0$ and precisely one type-$1$ edge and $|y_i|-1$ type $2$ edges if $y_i<0$. 

An edge in $E_A$ is directed towards the center and therefore towards its
smaller endpoint. Every other edge is directed towards its larger
endpoint. This proves the formula for~$t_A(j)$.

label: lem: column order
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Column order

title: Proof
body_md:
We first count inversions in a list containing all
vertices, and then subtract the inversions involving roots.

Consider $(z_0,\ldots,z_{\bar k}\mid t_A(1),\ldots,t_A(m))$.
The vertical bar merely separates the roots from the targets. The roots
remain in component order, and the targets remain in edge-label order.
Every vertex occurs exactly once: roots have indegree zero, and every
other vertex is the target of precisely one edge.

For the natural orientation, this list is $ (c_0,\ldots,c_{\bar k}\mid
 t_{\mathcal N}(1),\ldots,t_{\mathcal N}(m))$,
which is the increasing list of all vertices. Its inversion number is
therefore zero.

Now move a root along the path from its center to its prescribed position.
Suppose one step moves the current root from $u$ to an adjacent vertex $v$,
across edge $\ell$. Before this move, the edge points from $u$ to $v$, so
the root entry is $u$ and the entry corresponding to edge $\ell$ is $v$.
Afterwards, the root entry is $v$, while the reversed edge has target $u$.
Thus this move exchanges exactly two entries of the list.
All other entries remain unchanged.

Exchanging two entries reverses the parity of the inversion number, even
when their positions are not adjacent. Consequently, after moving all roots,
\begin{equation}\label{eq: sign of augmented list}
 \operatorname{inv}(z_0,\ldots,z_{\bar k},t_A(1),\ldots,t_A(m))
 \equiv |E_A|
 =\sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}|y_j|\pmod2.
\end{equation}
This is a parity statement: one move need not change the inversion number
by exactly one.

We now separate the inversions of this full list into three kinds:
\begin{itemize}
 \item inversions between two roots;
 \item inversions between a root and a target;
 \item inversions between two targets.
\end{itemize}
The last kind is precisely what the lemma seeks to count.

For the first kind, recall that $b_j=\bigl|\{i:i>j,\ z_i>z_j\}\bigr|$.
Thus $b_j$ counts the non-inversions whose first entry is $z_j$
in the root list. Since the roots are distinct, each of the
$\binom{\bar k+1}{2}$ pairs is either an inversion or a non-inversion.
Hence
\[
 \operatorname{inv}(z_0,\ldots,z_{\bar k})
 =\binom{\bar k+1}{2}-\sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}b_j.
\]

For the second kind, every root appears before every target. Therefore a
root $z_j$ and a target form an inversion exactly when the target is smaller
than $z_j$.
Since the vertices are consecutive with smallest vertex $|h^++h^-|$,
there are exactly $z_j-|h^++h^-|$
vertices smaller than $z_j$. Some are roots, so the number of targets
smaller than $z_j$ is $ z_j-|h^++h^-|-\bigl|\{i:z_i<z_j\}\bigr|$. Here, the last set includes all smaller roots, regardless of their
indices as these are never targets of an edge.
When we sum this expression over the components $j$, each unordered pair of roots contributes exactly once to the subtracted term: its smaller member is counted for its larger member.
Thus $ \sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}\bigl|\{i:z_i<z_j\}\bigr|
 =\binom{\bar k+1}{2}.$
The number of root--target inversions is consequently
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}(z_j-|h^++h^-|)-\binom{\bar k+1}{2}.
\]

Combining the three contributions gives the exact equality
\begin{equation*}
    \operatorname{inv}(z_0,\ldots,z_{\bar k},t_A(1),\ldots,t_A(m))=\operatorname{inv}(t_A(1),\ldots,t_A(m))
 +\sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}\bigl(z_j-|h^++h^-|-b_j\bigr).
\end{equation*}
The two binomial coefficients have cancelled. Reducing modulo $2$, and
using the root-move argument, yields
\[
 \operatorname{inv}(t_A(1),\ldots,t_A(m))
 \equiv\sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}
 \bigl(|y_j|+z_j-|h^++h^-|+b_j\bigr)\pmod2.
\]
The remaining step in the lemma is just substitution. From the definition
of $z_j$,
\[
 |y_j|+z_j-|h^++h^-|
 =\begin{cases}
 (K+1)y_j+j,&y_j\geq0,\\
 -(K+1)y_j-j-2|h^++h^-|,&y_j<0.
 \end{cases}
\]
Modulo $2$, this becomes
\[
 (K-1)y_j+j+2|h^++h^-|[y_j<0].
\]
Substituting into the above and using
$\sum_{j=0}^{\bar k}j=\binom{\bar k+1}{2}$ gives the asserted sign.

name: Determinant expansion

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem: Noodle-Doodle expansion first form} with
\[
 f_i=\xi_i,\qquad p_t(j)=p_+(j),\qquad
 p_s(j)=\epsilon^{[j\text{ is type }2]}p_-(j).
\]
This is valid also when the reflected argument is zero, since
$\xi_i(0)=\epsilon\xi_i(0)$. The factor contributed by the reflected
arguments is $\epsilon^{|E_A^2|}$, with $|E_A^2|$ given
by~\eqref{eq: tA(j) is equal to}. Every non-root vertex has indegree one,
so the set of targets is $V\setminus\{z_0,\ldots,z_{\bar k}\}$.
Parametrise the roots by~\eqref{eq: parametrisation of roots} and apply
Lemma~\ref{lem: column order} to put the columns in increasing order.

label: de:lambda(nu)
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{de:lambda(nu)}
    Let $
u$ be a composition and suppose that $\lambda$ and $\mathrm{sort}(
u) = \mu+ho_k$ are related in any of the above equivalent ways. Then, we write $\lambda = \lambda(
u)$. See Figure~ef{fig:flip}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Start by supposing $(\lambda+\rho_n) \sqcup (\mu+\rho_k) = \rho_{n+k}$.
    We are going to construct the following illustration step by step, where $\lambda$ is in yellow $\ytableaushort[*(yellow)]{{\circ}}$ and $\mathrm{flip}_{k^n}\mu$ in blue~$\ytableaushort[*(blue!20)]{{\cdot}}$. Once we are done, we will have established (1) implies (2).
    \[
    \ytableausetup{boxsize=.8em}
    \ydiagram[*(lightgray)]{1+8,2+7,3+6,4+5,5+4,6+3,7+2,8+1}
    \quad \leadsto \cdots \leadsto
    \ydiagram{1+8,2+7,3+6,4+5,5+4,6+3,7+2,8+1}*[*(lightgray)]{0,2+5,3+4,4+3,5+2,6+1}*[\cdot]{8+1,7+2,7+2,7+2}*[*(blue!20)]{8+1,7+2,7+2,7+2}*[\circ]{4+4,4+4}*[*(yellow)]{4+4,4+4}
    \quad \leadsto \cdots \leadsto
    \ydiagram{1+8,2+7,3+6,4+5,5+4,6+3,7+2,8+1}*[\cdot]{8+1,7+2,5+4,4+5}*[*(blue!20)]{8+1,7+2,5+4,4+5}*[\circ]{4+4,4+3,4+1}*[*(yellow)]{4+4,4+3,4+1}
    \]
    We start with a gray staircase $\rho_{n+k}$.

    In the first step, either $\mu_1+k-1 = n+k-1$ or $\lambda_1+n-1 = n+k-1$. In the first case, we have $\mu_1=n$, so we paint the first row with $k-1$ white and $n$ blue $\ytableaushort[*(blue!20)]{{\cdot}}$ cells. Otherwise, $\lambda_1=k$ and we color the last column with $k$ yellow $\ytableaushort[*(yellow)]{{\circ}}$ cells and $n-1$ white cells.

    In the $j$-th step, we have some $m$ rows and some $\ell$ columns with painted cells, and we are left with a gray staircase of size $n+k-m-\ell-1$.
    
    The biggest part of $\mu+\rho_k$ that we haven't used to color some row is $\mu_{m+1}+k-m-1$, and the biggest part of $\lambda+\rho_n$ not used in any column is $\lambda_{\ell+1}+n-\ell-1$. Either of these two quantities is equal to $n+k-m-\ell-1$, since this is the largest part of $\rho_{n+k}$ not still used in any row or column. Paint either the top row or the last column of the gray staircase accordingly. 
    
    After the $(n+k)$-th step, we get a $k\times n$ rectangle tiled by (translates of) $[\lambda]$ and $\mathrm{flip}_{k^n}\mu$.
    \medskip

    To go from (2) to (1), we reverse the algorithm: start with the full picture.
    Think of the boundary between blue $\ytableaushort[*(blue!20)]{{\cdot}}$  and yellow $\ytableaushort[*(yellow)]{{\circ}}$ cells as a lattice path from $(0,0)$ to $(k,n)$.
    Place a bullet at the $0$th coordinate of the lattice path, which is $(0,0)$.
    The first step is either north or east; move the bullet accordingly. 

    In the $j$-th step we have a gray staircase $\rho_j$ whose corner is touching the $j$-th coordinate of the lattice path. If the next step is north, then this means that $\lambda+\rho_n$ has a part of size~$j$; if the next step is east then this means that $\mu+\rho_k$ has a part of size~$j$. In either case, move the bullet point and grow the gray staircase accordingly.
    \[
    \ydiagram{1+8,2+7,3+6,4+5,5+4,6+3,7+2,8+1}*[*(lightgray)]{0,2+5,3+4,4+3,5+2,6+1}*[\cdot]{8+1,7+2,7+2,7+2}*[*(blue!20)]{8+1,7+2,7+2,7+2}*[\circ]{4+4,4+4}*[*(yellow)]{4+4,4+4}
    \begin{tikzpicture}[remember picture, overlay, x=.85em, y=.85em, xshift=0em, yshift=.2em]
                                  
        \fill[white, opacity=.3] (-8,-4) rectangle (0.1,4.1);
                   
        \draw[ultra thick] (-5,0) -- (-5,1) -- (-4,1) -- (-4,2) -- (-2,2) -- (-2,3) -- (-1,3) -- (-1,4) -- (0,4);
        \filldraw[fill=red, thick] (-2,3) circle (3pt);
    \end{tikzpicture}
    \]
    When the bullet arrives to $(k,n)$, we have that seen that all the possible sizes of parts $\{1, 2, \ldots, n+k-1\}$ that form $\rho_{n+k}$ are either coming from $\lambda+\rho_n$ or from $\mu+\rho_k$.\medskip

    That (2) and (3) are equivalent is clear from the definitions. Similarly, (4) and (5) are clearly equivalent. It remains thus to show (2) and (4) are equivalent.\medskip

    To show that (2) and (4) are equivalent, we come back to the lattice path defined above, which separates $[\lambda]$ from $\mathrm{flip}_{k^n}\mu$. The multiplicity $m_i(\lambda)$ is given by the number of north steps after the $i$-th east step of this path. But this is also counted by the difference of two consecutive parts of $\mu$, as claimed.

label: cor:useful.complementary
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:useful.complementary}
    Fix $c\in\mathbb{Z}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}$.
    Let $\epsilon \in \{\pm1\}$ and consider a family $\{\xi_i(m) \mid i\in[n],~m\in\mathbb{Z}+c\}$ of elements of a ring $R$.
    Let $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ be a partition. If $\lambda = \lambda(\nu)$ then
    \[
    (-1)^{\binom{n}{2}}\det_{1\le i,j \le n}(\xi_i(\lambda_j + n-j + c)) = \det_{\substack{1\le i\le n \\ j\in([0,n+k-1]+c)\setminus\{\nu_a+c \mid a=1,\dots,k\}}}(\xi_i(j))^{1\le i\le n}.
    \]
    The converse also holds if there are no non-trivial algebraic relations between the $\{\xi_i(m) \mid i\in[n],~m\in\mathbb{Z}+c\}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\lambda = \lambda(\nu)$ then the identity is clear after noting that in the left-hand side the arguments are in decreasing order in $j$, whereas the arguments on the right-hand side are in increasing order; reordering columns we obtain a sign $(-1)^{\binom{n}{2}}$.

    Let us now prove the reciprocal.
    Since there are no algebraic relations between the $\xi_i(m)$ the equality of determinants implies the following identity of the arguments on the left and right-hand sides:
    \[
    \{\lambda_j + n - j + c \mid j=1,\ldots,n\} = ([0,n+k-1]+c)\setminus\{\nu_a+c ~\mid~ a=1,\dots,k\}.
    \]
    Cancel the summand of $c$ from the three sets. If $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n)$ is a partition then the left-hand side becomes the multiset of parts of $\lambda + \rho_n$. 
    On the right-hand side, note that $[0,n+k-1]$ is the set of parts of $\rho_{n+k}$. Hence if $\nu = (\nu_1, \ldots, \nu_k)$ is a composition then we have
    \[
    (\lambda + \rho_n) \sqcup \nu = \rho_{n+k},
    \]
    which is to say $\lambda = \lambda(\nu)$ as claimed.

label: lem: handling the summation range
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: handling the summation range}
Let $n,k\in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$, $
u\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^k$ then $\lambda(
u)$ is a partition inside $(k^n)$ if and only if $
u_1,\dots,
u_k\in[0,n+k-1]$ are all different elements. For the determinant expressions below, we use $\lambda(
u)'_i=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}+i-1$ even if this sequence is not a partition. Furthermore, we have that
 egin{align*}
     \det\limits_{1\le i,j\le k}(\dot e_{\lambda(
u)'_i-i+j}+ \dot e_{\lambda(
u)'_i-i-j+1})&=so_{\lambda(
u)}(X)\
    \det\limits_{1\le i,j\le k}(\dot e_{\lambda(
u)'_i-i+j}-\dot  e_{\lambda(
u)'_i-i-j})&=sp_{\lambda(
u)}(X)\
     rac{1}{2}\det\limits_{1\le i,j\le k}(\dot e_{\lambda(
u)'_i-i+j} +\dot e_{\lambda(
u)'_i-i-j+2})&=o^{	extup{even}}_{\lambda(
u)}(X)\qquad(k\geq1).
\end{align*}
if $
u_1,\dots,
u_k\in[0,n+k-1]$ are all different elements and otherwise the left hand side of each of these equations is zero. Note that the right hand side is then zero too by \eqref{eq: convention not a partiton} so equality still holds.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k=0$, the first assertion and the first two identities are immediate, with empty determinants equal to $1$. We may therefore assume that $k\geq1$.

    First assume that $\lambda(
u)$ is a partition inside $(k^n)$, thus $\lambda(
u)'$ is a partition inside $(n^k)$. By definition we have that $\lambda(
u)'_i=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}+i-1\in[0,n],$
    thus $\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}\in[i-1,n+i-1]$. Therefore, all parts $
u_1,\dots,
u_k$ are inside $[0,n+k-1]$. Assume two of them were equal, then there exists $i_1\in[1,k-1]$ such that $\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i_1}=\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k-i_1}$. But then we have that $$\lambda(
u)'_{i_1}=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i_1}+i_1-1<n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k-i_1}+i_1=\lambda(
u)'_{i_1+1},$$
    and thus $\lambda(
u)'$ and subsequently $\lambda(
u)$ would not be partitions. This contradicts our assumption and thus $
u_1,\dots
u_k$ all have to be different elements. 

    Now assume that $
u_1,\dots,
u_k\in[0,n+k-1]$ are all different elements. Then $i-1\leq \mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}\leq n+i-1$ and hence $n\geq \lambda(
u)_i'=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}+i-1\geq 0$ and is weakly decreasing as 
    $$\lambda(
u)_i'=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}+i-1\geq n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k-i}+i=\lambda(
u)_{i+1}',$$
    for $1\leq i<k$, as $\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-i}+1\leq \mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k-i}$ because all the $
u_i$ are different. Therefore $\lambda(
u)'$ is a partition inside $(n^k)$ and so $\lambda(
u)$ is a partition inside $(k^n)$.

    To prove the claim about the determinants, first note that if $
u_1,\dots,
u_k\in[0,n+k-1]$ are all different elements then $\lambda(
u)$ is a partition as we just proved and then the formulae are just the dual Jacobi--Trudi identities from \eqref{eq: dual JT type B}, \eqref{eq: dual JT type C} and \eqref{eq: dual JT type D}. If the condition is not satisfied then there either exist $i,i'\in[1,k]$ with $i
eq i'$ such that $
u_i=
u_{i'}$ or there exists an $i\in[1,k]$ such that $
u_i\geq n+k$. 
    
    In the first case we then have that there exists an $\ell\in[1,k-1]$ such that $\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-\ell}=\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k-\ell}$. Therefore
    $$\lambda(
u)'_{\ell}=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k+1-\ell}+\ell-1=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{k-\ell}+\ell-1=\lambda(
u)'_{\ell+1}-1,$$
    and thus $\lambda(
u)'_\ell-\ell=\lambda(
u)'_{\ell+1}-(\ell+1)$. Therefore the $\ell$-th and $(\ell+1)$-st rows of each of the three matrices agree. Hence the determinant vanishes and the left hand side is zero in each of the three cases.

    In the second case we get that $\mathrm{sort}(
u)_1\geq n+k$. Therefore, we have $\lambda(
u)'_k=n-\mathrm{sort}(
u)_{1}+k-1\leq -1$. For $1\leq j\leq k$, we have
    \[
    \lambda(
u)'_k-k+j\leq\lambda(
u)'_k\leq-1,
    \qquad
    \lambda(
u)'_k-k-j+2\leq\lambda(
u)'_k-k+1\leq-1.
    \]
    Thus all indices in the $k$-th row of each of the three matrices are negative, and so this row vanishes since $\dot e_r=0$ for $r<0$. Then also the determinant vanishes and the left hand side is again zero in all three cases.
